Confusable pairs among the occupant-protection rules; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec03-R01 | anchor: A01
Age two marks the rear-facing back-seat rule, age six marks both the start of the adult belt requirement and the end of the under-six restraint rule, though a child still under 57 inches keeps needing a restraint. [A01]
Why it matters: group child restraints; confusable age two versus age six versus height.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-R02 | anchor: A01
The unattended-child rule protects children aged 7 or younger, and the only exception is supervision by someone at least 12 years old who keeps the child in sight. [A01]
Why it matters: group unattended occupants; confusable seven versus twelve.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-R03 | anchor: A01
Model year 1968 brought lap belts for front-seat passengers, while model year 1970 brought lap belts for every passenger and front-seat shoulder harnesses. [A01]
Why it matters: group belt equipment; confusable 1968 versus 1970.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-R04 | anchor: A01
For children, the restraint law reaches the driver's license itself, since failing to restrain a young child can bring a license suspension as well as fines or community service. [A01]
Why it matters: group penalties; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-R05 | anchor: A01
The unattended-child rule turns on significant risk to the child's health and safety, while the dog-or-cat rule turns on extreme heat or cold; both are misdemeanors. [A01]
Why it matters: group unattended occupants; confusable child versus pet trigger.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-R06 | anchor: A02
Older children may ride up front only when necessary and with the seat pushed fully back, but an infant may never ride in front of a passenger-side airbag. [A02]
Why it matters: group seating; confusable older child versus infant in front.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-R07 | anchor: A02
A booster or belt-positioning seat works with the vehicle's own seat belt, while a rear-facing seat holds the infant itself and protects the head, neck and spine. [A02]
Why it matters: group child restraints; confusable booster versus rear-facing seat.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-R08 | anchor: A02
Safe child travel needs three checks: a DOT-approved restraint, a seat that fits the child's size and weight, and an installation that follows the manufacturer or NHTSA. [A02]
Why it matters: group child restraints; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0026]
